summary: Former BC Forest Service fire lookout on Brent Mountain, 22 km west of Penticton; used as a warming hut when required, in a protected area reached by a 5 km trail.

facts.agency: BC Forest Service (former lookout operator); BC Parks (protected area)

access.note: The protected area is used for hiking, horse use and snowmobiling; BC Parks says the lookout is used as a warming hut when required.

visit.trail_note: Summit trail roughly 5 km; allow four to five hours return; BC Parks recommends high clearance on the access road.

evidence.supports: Lookout is 22 km west of Penticton, in the protected area
evidence.quote: Brent Mountain Protected Area is 22 km west of the city of Penticton.

evidence.supports: Former BC Forest Service fire lookout on the summit
evidence.quote: A former BC Forest Service fire lookout sits atop the Brent Mountain

evidence.supports: Lookout tower constructed in the 1930s on the summit to protect lumber (Peakvisor, not confirmed elsewhere)
evidence.quote: a fire lookout tower was constructed in the 1930s upon the summit of Mount Brent to help protect the region and its valuable lumber from fires

evidence.supports: BC Parks calls the lookout unused
evidence.quote: an unused Forest Service fire lookout

evidence.supports: Lookout used as a warming hut when required
evidence.quote: The Brent Mountain fire lookout is used as a warming hut when required.

evidence.supports: Blog calls the tower abandoned, with 360-degree views from the top
evidence.quote: What sets this hike apart is the incredible summit experience, with 360 views and an awesome abandoned fire lookout tower.
Brent Mountain Protected Area was established on April 18, 2001.
The Brent Mountain Trail is roughly 5 km.

evidence.supports: Allow four to five hours return
evidence.quote: Allow four to five hours return.

evidence.supports: Park gives 444 m of elevation gain
evidence.quote: after an elevation gain of 444 m

evidence.supports: Blog gives 490 m of elevation gain
BC Parks recommends high clearance for the access road, which has deep water bars
evidence.quote: A vehicle with high clearance is recommended as there are some deep water bars along the road.

evidence.supports: Drivers should be cautious of logging trucks
evidence.quote: be cautious of oncoming logging trucks

evidence.supports: Area used for hiking, horse use and snowmobiling
evidence.quote: This area provides a variety of regional outdoor recreational opportunities, including hiking, horse use and snowmobiling.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: BC Parks gives 444 m of elevation gain on the summit trail; the hiking blog gives 490 m. The story reports both.

notes_for_editor: The only construction claim is Peakvisor's 1930s, a decade with no exact year, so no built event is set. A Facebook group post in BC Forest Fire Lookouts reportedly gives 1931, but its text was not in the cache, so it is not cited. A search surfaced a Royal BC Museum series of Forest Service lookout photographs (GR-3263) and a Penticton museum as possible leads; neither was checked. BC Parks describes the lookout as unused and as a warming hut; no source says whether the interior is open to climbers. The registry entry (firelookout.ca) adds no detail beyond the location, so it is not cited.
